claim: Type II RAF inhibitors paradoxically activate BRAF at subsaturating concentrations.
source: The type II class of RAF inhibitors currently in clinical trials paradoxically activate BRAF at subsaturating concentrations.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known phenomenon that the study investigates.

claim: Paradoxical activation by type II inhibitors is mediated by induction of BRAF dimers.
source: Activation is mediated by induction of BRAF dimers, but why activation rather than inhibition occurs remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: For type II inhibitors, the allosteric coupling between inhibitor binding and BRAF dimerization is distributed asymmetrically across the two dimer binding sites.
source: For type II inhibitors the allosteric coupling between inhibitor binding and BRAF dimerization is distributed asymmetrically across the two dimer binding sites, with binding to the first site dominating the allostery.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by FRET experiments and global fitting analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Binding of type II inhibitors to the first site dominates the allosteric coupling.
source: For type II inhibitors the allosteric coupling between inhibitor binding and BRAF dimerization is distributed asymmetrically across the two dimer binding sites, with binding to the first site dominating the allostery.
evidence: This is supported by the large α values and small β values determined from global fitting analysis shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Allosteric asymmetry of type II inhibitors results in efficient and selective induction of dimers with one inhibited and one catalytically active subunit.
source: This asymmetry results in efficient and selective induction of dimers with one inhibited and one catalytically active subunit.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by simulations and kinase activity data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Type I inhibitors lack allosteric asymmetry.
source: Unlike type II inhibitors, type I inhibitors lack allosteric asymmetry and do not activate BRAF homodimers.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by α and β values shown in Figure 1f,g.

claim: Type I inhibitors do not activate BRAF homodimers.
source: Unlike type II inhibitors, type I inhibitors lack allosteric asymmetry and do not activate BRAF homodimers.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by kinase activity data in Figure 2 and cellular data in Figure 3.

claim: BRAF homodimers are dynamically asymmetric with only one of the subunits locked in the active αC-in state.
source: Finally, NMR data reveal that BRAF homodimers are dynamically asymmetric with only one of the subunits locked in the active αC-in state.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by 19F NMR data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Binding of only a single αC-in inhibitor molecule can induce potent BRAF dimerization and activation.
source: This provides a structural mechanism for how binding of only a single αC-in inhibitor molecule can induce potent BRAF dimerization and activation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an interpretation of the NMR data and allosteric coupling results.

claim: BRAF is a central component of the MAPK (RAF-MEK-ERK) signaling pathway.
source: The protein kinase BRAF is a central component of the MAPK (RAF-MEK-ERK) signaling pathway and plays a critical role in the regulation of eukaryotic cell growth, proliferation, and survival (Lavoie and Therrien, 2015; Wellbrock et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: BRAF plays a critical role in the regulation of eukaryotic cell growth, proliferation, and survival.
source: The protein kinase BRAF is a central component of the MAPK (RAF-MEK-ERK) signaling pathway and plays a critical role in the regulation of eukaryotic cell growth, proliferation, and survival (Lavoie and Therrien, 2015; Wellbrock et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: In quiescent cells, BRAF exists in the cytosol as an autoinhibited monomer.
source: In quiescent cells, BRAF exists in the cytosol as an autoinhibited monomer (Park et al., 2019; Martinez Fiesco et al., 2022; Thevakumaran et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Upon initiation of growth factor signaling, BRAF monomers are recruited to the plasma membrane by RAS-GTP.
source: Upon initiation of growth factor signaling, BRAF monomers are recruited to the plasma membrane by RAS-GTP and activated by homodimerization or by heterodimerization with the additional isoforms ARAF and CRAF (Rushworth et al., 2006; Weber et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: BRAF is activated by homodimerization or by heterodimerization with ARAF and CRAF.
source: Upon initiation of growth factor signaling, BRAF monomers are recruited to the plasma membrane by RAS-GTP and activated by homodimerization or by heterodimerization with the additional isoforms ARAF and CRAF (Rushworth et al., 2006; Weber et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Dimerization allosterically activates BRAF by triggering a conformational change of the regulatory αC-helix from an inactive αC-out state to an active αC-in state.
source: Dimerization allosterically activates BRAF by triggering a conformational change of the regulatory αC-helix from an inactive αC-out state to an active αC-in state (Rajakulendran et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Activated BRAF dimers initiate a phosphorylation cascade in which MEK and ERK are sequentially activated by successive phosphorylation events.
source: Activated BRAF dimers initiate a phosphorylation cascade in which MEK and ERK are sequentially activated by successive phosphorylation events (Lavoie and Therrien, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Mutations in BRAF play a major role in driving human cancers, most notably in approximately half of melanoma cases.
source: Mutations in BRAF play a major role in driving human cancers, most notably in approximately half of melanoma cases (Davies et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The most prevalent BRAF mutation is V600E.
source: The most prevalent BRAF mutation is V600E (Owsley et al., 2021), which confers constitutive kinase activity on BRAF by disrupting critical autoinhibitory interactions, allowing monomeric V600E BRAF to phosphorylate its substrate MEK independently of upstream signaling and dimerization (Yao et al., 2015; Wan et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: V600E mutation confers constitutive kinase activity on BRAF by disrupting critical autoinhibitory interactions.
source: The most prevalent BRAF mutation is V600E (Owsley et al., 2021), which confers constitutive kinase activity on BRAF by disrupting critical autoinhibitory interactions, allowing monomeric V600E BRAF to phosphorylate its substrate MEK independently of upstream signaling and dimerization (Yao et al., 2015; Wan et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Monomeric V600E BRAF can phosphorylate its substrate MEK independently of upstream signaling and dimerization.
source: The most prevalent BRAF mutation is V600E (Owsley et al., 2021), which confers constitutive kinase activity on BRAF by disrupting critical autoinhibitory interactions, allowing monomeric V600E BRAF to phosphorylate its substrate MEK independently of upstream signaling and dimerization (Yao et al., 2015; Wan et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: FDA-approved inhibitors vemurafenib, dabrafenib, and encorafenib show remarkable initial responses in V600E-driven metastatic melanoma patients.
source: The FDA-approved inhibitors vemurafenib, dabrafenib, and encorafenib show remarkable initial responses in V600E-driven metastatic melanoma patients due to their effective inhibition of V600E BRAF monomers.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established clinical knowledge.

claim: Clinical resistance to FDA-approved BRAF inhibitors emerges rapidly and is driven by the formation of mutant BRAF dimers.
source: However, clinical resistance emerges rapidly and is driven by the formation of mutant BRAF dimers, which these drugs fail to inhibit (Chapman et al., 2011; Hauschild et al., 2012; Dummer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: FDA-approved BRAF inhibitors fail to inhibit mutant BRAF dimers.
source: However, clinical resistance emerges rapidly and is driven by the formation of mutant BRAF dimers, which these drugs fail to inhibit (Chapman et al., 2011; Hauschild et al., 2012; Dummer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Mechanisms that promote BRAF dimerization confer resistance to FDA-approved BRAF inhibitors.
source: Consequently, mechanisms that promote BRAF dimerization, including receptor tyrosine kinase upregulation, activating RAS mutations, and BRAF splice variants, confer resistance to these inhibitors (Nazarian et al., 2010; Poulikakos et al., 2011; Wagle et al., 2011; Cook and Cook, 2021; Proietti et al., 2020; Brummer and McInnes, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: FDA-approved BRAF inhibitors can paradoxically activate BRAF dimers, leading to elevated MAPK signaling in cells containing dimeric BRAF.
source: In fact, these inhibitors can paradoxically activate BRAF dimers, leading to elevated MAPK signaling in cells containing dimeric BRAF (Poulikakos et al., 2010; Hatzivassiliou et al., 2010; Joseph et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Paradoxical activation by FDA-approved BRAF inhibitors triggers the emergence of secondary cutaneous carcinomas in many patients.
source: This paradoxical activation triggers the emergence of secondary cutaneous carcinomas in many patients treated with these inhibitors (Su et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The failure of FDA-approved BRAF inhibitors to block BRAF dimers is attributed to negative allostery.
source: The failure of the FDA-approved BRAF inhibitors to block BRAF dimers is attributed to negative allostery, in which inhibitors preferentially bind the inactive αC-out state of BRAF and are unable to bind to the active αC-in state adopted by BRAF dimers (Karoulia et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: FDA-approved BRAF inhibitors preferentially bind the inactive αC-out state of BRAF and are unable to bind to the active αC-in state adopted by BRAF dimers.
source: The failure of the FDA-approved BRAF inhibitors to block BRAF dimers is attributed to negative allostery, in which inhibitors preferentially bind the inactive αC-out state of BRAF and are unable to bind to the active αC-in state adopted by BRAF dimers (Karoulia et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: A new class of inhibitors that recognize the αC-in state and bypass negative allostery has been developed.
source: This discovery prompted the development of a new class of inhibitors that recognize the αC-in state and bypass this negative allostery (Peng et al., 2015; Okaniwa et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: αC-in inhibitors bind to both subunits of the BRAF dimer in X-ray structures.
source: Remarkably, despite binding to both subunits of the BRAF dimer in X-ray structures (Peng et al., 2015; Yen et al., 2021; Tkacik et al., 2023) and being reportedly equipotent for both subunits (Cotto-Rios et al., 2020), these αC-in inhibitors still induce paradoxical activation of MAPK/ERK signaling in cells (Poulikakos et al., 2010; Yen et al., 2021; Cotto-Rios et al., 2020; Hall-Jackson et al., 1999; Nakamura et al., 2013; Lai et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: αC-in inhibitors are reportedly equipotent for both subunits of the BRAF dimer.
source: Remarkably, despite binding to both subunits of the BRAF dimer in X-ray structures (Peng et al., 2015; Yen et al., 2021; Tkacik et al., 2023) and being reportedly equipotent for both subunits (Cotto-Rios et al., 2020), these αC-in inhibitors still induce paradoxical activation of MAPK/ERK signaling in cells (Poulikakos et al., 2010; Yen et al., 2021; Cotto-Rios et al., 2020; Hall-Jackson et al., 1999; Nakamura et al., 2013; Lai et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: αC-in inhibitors induce paradoxical activation of MAPK/ERK signaling in cells.
source: Remarkably, despite binding to both subunits of the BRAF dimer in X-ray structures (Peng et al., 2015; Yen et al., 2021; Tkacik et al., 2023) and being reportedly equipotent for both subunits (Cotto-Rios et al., 2020), these αC-in inhibitors still induce paradoxical activation of MAPK/ERK signaling in cells (Poulikakos et al., 2010; Yen et al., 2021; Cotto-Rios et al., 2020; Hall-Jackson et al., 1999; Nakamura et al., 2013; Lai et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Paradoxical activation by αC-in inhibitors is linked to their ability to induce BRAF dimers.
source: Paradoxical activation by αC-in inhibitors is linked to their ability to induce BRAF dimers (Lavoie et al., 2013), but the molecular mechanisms triggering this activation remain elusive.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The baseline dimerization affinity of apo BRAF (KDdimer) was found to be 62.4±2.9 μM.
source: In control experiments without drug, the baseline dimerization affinity of apo BRAF (KDdimer) was found to be 62.4±2.9 μM, in agreement with previously reported values (Lavoie et al., 2013; Figure 1—figure supplement 2a and b).
evidence: This is a measured value from FRET experiments reported in the Results section.

claim: All αC-in inhibitors induced large increases in the A/D ratio, consistent with inhibitor-induced BRAF dimerization.
source: All αC-in inhibitors induced large increases in the A/D ratio, consistent with inhibitor-induced BRAF dimerization (Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a direct observation from FRET experiments shown in Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Inhibitor-bound BRAF dimerizes with nanomolar affinity.
source: The change in A/D ratio with BRAF concentration observed at saturating inhibitor concentrations indicated that inhibitor-bound BRAF dimerizes with nanomolar affinity, representing several orders of magnitude enhancement over baseline dimerization.
evidence: This is inferred from FRET data analysis described in the Results section.

claim: For type II inhibitors, the allosteric coupling factor α is as large as 10^4.
source: Rather, these drugs are coupled to BRAF dimerization in a highly asymmetric manner, with the large majority of dimer promotion provided by the binding of the first inhibitor molecule (α values as large as 104), and the contributions from the second inhibitor molecule being orders of magnitude smaller (β values no larger than 102) (Figure 1f and g and Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a result from global fitting analysis shown in Figure 1f.

claim: For type II inhibitors, the allosteric coupling factor β is no larger than 10^2.
source: Rather, these drugs are coupled to BRAF dimerization in a highly asymmetric manner, with the large majority of dimer promotion provided by the binding of the first inhibitor molecule (α values as large as 104), and the contributions from the second inhibitor molecule being orders of magnitude smaller (β values no larger than 102) (Figure 1f and g and Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a result from global fitting analysis shown in Figure 1f.

claim: For type I inhibitors, the α and β values are approximately equal.
source: In contrast, the allosteric coupling for the type I inhibitors is symmetrical (Figure 1g), with the α and β values being approximately equal (Figure 1f and Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is a result from global fitting analysis shown in Figure 1f,g.

claim: For many type II inhibitors, the large α values boost affinities for the first dimer subunit into the picomolar range.
source: For many of the type II inhibitors the large α values boost affinities for the first dimer subunit into the picomolar range while the affinities for the second subunit are substantially weaker.
evidence: This is calculated from the allosteric model parameters determined by global fitting.

claim: Type I inhibitors bind the first and second subunits of the dimer with comparable affinity.
source: In contrast, type I inhibitors, which have similar α and β values, bind the first and second subunits of the dimer with comparable affinity (Figure 1e and Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is inferred from the similar α and β values shown in Figure 1e and Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: Type II inhibitors triggered increases in the A/D ratios similar in magnitude to those observed in BRAF:BRAF experiments when tested with BRAF^A481F:BRAF heterodimers.
source: In these experiments, type II inhibitors triggered increases in the A/D ratios similar in magnitude to those observed in a donor-matched BRAF:BRAF experiment, indicating a similar extent of dimer induction (Figure 1—figure supplement 9a).
evidence: This is a direct observation from FRET experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 9a.

claim: Dimerization affinities of type II inhibitors at saturating concentrations were in the low nanomolar range in BRAF^A481F:BRAF heterodimer experiments.
source: Furthermore, dimerization affinities at saturating inhibitor concentrations were in the low nanomolar range, corresponding to a fold-increase over baseline dimerization of between 103 and 104, in good agreement with our measured α values for the type II inhibitors (Figure 1—figure supplement 9b).
evidence: This is measured from FRET experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 9b.

claim: The type I inhibitor GDC0879 failed to induce BRAF^A481F:BRAF heterodimers.
source: The type I inhibitor GDC0879, which possesses a far more modest α value (Figure 1f), failed to induce BRAFA481F:BRAF heterodimers in this experiment.
evidence: This is a direct observation from FRET experiments described in the Results section.

claim: All three αC-out inhibitors disrupted BRAF dimerization to such an extent that no dimerization signal was observed at saturating inhibitor concentrations.
source: All three disrupted dimerization to such an extent that no dimerization signal was observed at saturating inhibitor concentrations, preventing the global fit analysis from converging to a constrained solution.
evidence: This is a direct observation from FRET experiments described in the Results section.

claim: Dimer disruption by αC-out inhibitors is weaker than dimer promotion by αC-in inhibitors, with total decreases in dimerization affinity of 1–2 orders of magnitude.
source: This analysis showed that dimer disruption by αC-out inhibitors is weaker than dimer promotion by αC-in inhibitors, with total decreases in dimerization affinity of 1–2 orders of magnitude (Figure 1f and Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is a result from global fitting analysis shown in Figure 1f and Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: For all αC-in inhibitors, simulations predict a bell-shaped curve for the induction of partially occupied BBD dimers.
source: For all αC-in inhibitors, simulations predict a bell-shaped curve for the induction of partially occupied BBD dimers that increases with inhibitor concentration and peaks at approximately a 1:2 molar ratio of inhibitor to BRAF, before decreasing at higher concentrations due to the formation of dimers saturated with inhibitor (BBDD) (Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a prediction from simulations using the parameterized allosteric models shown in Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: BBD induction amplitudes for type II inhibitors varied from 11% to 78% of total BRAF protein.
source: The BBD induction amplitudes varied for type II inhibitors from 11% to 78% of total BRAF protein, but as a group were substantially higher than the amplitudes associated with the type I inhibitors which ranged from 4% to 11% (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is a result from simulations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a.

claim: BBD induction amplitudes for type I inhibitors ranged from 4% to 11%.
source: The BBD induction amplitudes varied for type II inhibitors from 11% to 78% of total BRAF protein, but as a group were substantially higher than the amplitudes associated with the type I inhibitors which ranged from 4% to 11% (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is a result from simulations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a.

claim: The amplitude of BBD induction is primarily dictated by the ratio between α and β, following a hyperbolic relationship with respect to α/β.
source: This analysis revealed that the amplitude of BBD induction is primarily dictated by the ratio between α and β, or the degree of asymmetry in the allosteric model, following a hyperbolic relationship with respect to α/β (Figure 2c), rather than by the total magnitude of dimer enhancement (αβ).
evidence: This is a result from simulations shown in Figure 2b,c.

claim: Type II inhibitors induced strong dose-dependent increases in BRAF activity up to 19-fold above the no-inhibitor control.
source: In this assay, type II inhibitors induced strong dose-dependent increases in BRAF activity up to 19-fold above the no-inhibitor control that agreed strikingly well with simulated BBD induction curves (Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and 2b ).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from kinase activity assays shown in Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and 2b.

claim: Type I inhibitors induced only relatively minor increases in BRAF activity.
source: In contrast, the type I inhibitors induced only relatively minor increases in BRAF activity (Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and 2b ), consistent with their weak ability to induce BBD dimers, and the αC-out inhibitors vemurafenib and dabrafenib failed to trigger any discernable activation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from kinase activity assays shown in Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and 2b.

claim: The αC-out inhibitors vemurafenib and dabrafenib failed to trigger any discernable BRAF activation.
source: In contrast, the type I inhibitors induced only relatively minor increases in BRAF activity (Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and 2b ), consistent with their weak ability to induce BBD dimers, and the αC-out inhibitors vemurafenib and dabrafenib failed to trigger any discernable activation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from kinase activity assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is a linear correlation (R2=0.93) between measured amplitudes of kinase activation and BBD induction amplitudes predicted by the parameterized allosteric models.
source: Comparing the measured amplitudes of kinase activation with the BBD induction amplitudes predicted by the parameterized allosteric models for each inhibitor revealed an impressive linear correlation (R2=0.93) (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is a result from comparing kinase activity data with model predictions shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The slope of the linear fit between kinase activation and BBD induction yielded a catalytic turnover per BBD dimer of (3.2±0.3) × 10^–3 s^–1.
source: The slope of the linear fit yielded a value for the catalytic turnover per BBD dimer of (3.2±0.3) × 10–3 s–1.
evidence: This is calculated from the linear fit shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The catalytic turnover per BBD dimer is in excellent agreement with the turnover value of 4.5×10^–3 s^–1 for drug-free BRAF dimers bound to 14-3-3.
source: This value is in excellent agreement with the turnover value of 4.5×10–3 s–1 for drug-free BRAF dimers bound to 14-3-3 reported by Liau et al., 2020.
evidence: This is a comparison with published data cited from Liau et al., 2020.

claim: Partially occupied BRAF dimers are highly active and minimally impacted by the presence of one αC-in inhibitor molecule.
source: This observation shows that partially occupied BRAF dimers are highly active and minimally impacted by the presence of one αC-in inhibitor molecule, and that the amplitude of paradoxical activation is directly determined by the concentration of this dimer species.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of measured turnover with published values for fully active BRAF dimers.

claim: The amplitude of paradoxical activation is directly determined by the concentration of BBD dimer species.
source: This observation shows that partially occupied BRAF dimers are highly active and minimally impacted by the presence of one αC-in inhibitor molecule, and that the amplitude of paradoxical activation is directly determined by the concentration of this dimer species.
evidence: This is inferred from the linear correlation between BBD induction and kinase activity shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The type I inhibitor GDC0879 induced a shorter average spin-spin distance than the type II inhibitors AZ628, LY3009120, and TAK632 in DEER experiments.
source: However, the type I inhibitor GDC0879 induced a shorter average spin-spin distance than the type II inhibitors AZ628, LY3009120, and TAK632, which yielded distance distributions that were intermediate between those observed with GDC0879 and with apo BRAF (Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is a direct observation from DEER spectroscopy data shown in Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Type I and type II inhibitors induce distinct αC-helix conformations in solution.
source: These data confirm that the different binding modes of type I and type II inhibitors are associated with distinct αC-helix conformations.
evidence: This is concluded from DEER spectroscopy data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The type II inhibitors in the dataset all induced dose-dependent increases of pMEK1/2 and pERK1/2 indicating activation of the MAPK signaling pathway.
source: The type II inhibitors in our dataset all induced dose-dependent increases of pMEK1/2 and pERK1/2 indicating activation of the MAPK signaling pathway (Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Poulikakos et al., 2010; Karoulia et al., 2016; Yen et al., 2021; Cotto-Rios et al., 2020; Lavoie et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a direct observation from flow cytometry experiments shown in Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Many type II inhibitors activate the MAPK/ERK signaling pathway at inhibitor concentrations below 1 nM.
source: First, many type II inhibitors activate the MAPK/ERK signaling pathway at inhibitor concentrations below 1 nM, consistent with ultrapotent inhibitor binding to the first site on the dimer that arises from the extreme allosteric coupling between inhibitor and BRAF dimerization (Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 2 ).
evidence: This is observed in flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The concentrations at which activation and inhibition occur by type II inhibitors differ by several orders of magnitude.
source: Second, the concentrations at which activation and inhibition occur differ by several orders of magnitude.
evidence: This is observed in flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: MAPK pathway activation by the type I inhibitors GDC0879, SB590885, and L779450 was observed in SK-MEL-2 cells across a wide concentration range.
source: Nonetheless, we observed MAPK pathway activation by the type I inhibitors GDC0879, SB590885, and L779450 in SK-MEL-2 cells (Figure 3d right panel and Figure 3—figure supplement 2) across a wide concentration range, as seen with the type II inhibitors.
evidence: This is a direct observation from flow cytometry experiments shown in Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: MAPK activation by type I inhibitors is not mediated by BRAF homodimers but instead by BRAF:CRAF heterodimers.
source: This discrepancy suggests that MAPK activation by type I inhibitors is not mediated by BRAF homodimers but instead by BRAF:CRAF heterodimers.
evidence: This is inferred from the discrepancy between predicted and observed activation windows for type I inhibitors.

claim: Activation by GDC0879 depends on the presence of CRAF.
source: In support of this, activation by GDC0879 depends on the presence of CRAF (Hatzivassiliou et al., 2010), and both GDC0879 and SB590885 promote BRAF:CRAF heterodimers to a greater extent than the type II inhibitors AZ628 and sorafenib (Hatzivassiliou et al., 2010; Jin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: GDC0879 and SB590885 promote BRAF:CRAF heterodimers to a greater extent than the type II inhibitors AZ628 and sorafenib.
source: In support of this, activation by GDC0879 depends on the presence of CRAF (Hatzivassiliou et al., 2010), and both GDC0879 and SB590885 promote BRAF:CRAF heterodimers to a greater extent than the type II inhibitors AZ628 and sorafenib (Hatzivassiliou et al., 2010; Jin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Type I inhibitors are less effective at inhibiting CRAF than type II inhibitors.
source: Furthermore, type I inhibitors are less effective at inhibiting CRAF than type II inhibitors, preventing them from fully inhibiting the BRAF:CRAF heterodimers they induce (Hatzivassiliou et al., 2010; Heidorn et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: SK-MEL-2 cells express all RAF isoforms at comparable levels.
source: We have confirmed by immunoblot that SK-MEL-2 cells express all RAF isoforms at comparable levels, indicating that activation through BRAF:CRAF heterodimers is a plausible model for these inhibitors (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a direct observation from immunoblot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Spectra of labeled apo BRAF showed two well-resolved resonances at –84.29 and –84.42 ppm in 19F NMR.
source: Spectra of labeled apo BRAF showed two well-resolved resonances at –84.29 and –84.42 ppm (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a direct observation from 19F NMR experiments shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The upfield resonance in 19F NMR was defined as the αC-out (monomeric) state and the downfield resonance as the αC-in (dimeric) state.
source: Resonance assignment was achieved by adding saturating concentrations of ATP, known to induce the αC-out state. From this, the upfield resonance was defined as the αC-out (monomeric) state and the downfield resonance as the αC-in (dimeric) state (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is determined from ATP titration experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Increasing the concentration of BRAF led to an increase in the αC-in peak area and a relative decrease in the αC-out peak area that fit to a monomer-dimer equilibrium with a KD of 32.2±9.4 μM.
source: Increasing the concentration of BRAF led to an increase in the αC-in peak area and a relative decrease in the αC-out peak area that fit to a monomer-dimer equilibrium with a KD of 32.2±9.4 μM, in reasonable agreement with the FRET experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is measured from 19F NMR experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Spectral deconvolution of the apo BRAF 19F NMR data revealed an additional resonance underneath the αC-in peak.
source: Spectral deconvolution of the apo BRAF data revealed an additional resonance underneath the αC-in peak (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a result from spectral deconvolution analysis shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The αC-in^broad resonance is substantially exchange-broadened, with a fitted line width approximately five times that of the αC-in^narrow resonance.
source: This second αC-in resonance, referred to as 'αC-inbroad', is substantially exchange-broadened, with a fitted line width approximately five times that of the narrower overlapping αC-in resonance, hereafter referred to as 'αC-innarrow' (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is measured from spectral deconvolution shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1d.

claim: The short relaxation time of the αC-in^broad resonance (<5 ms) is consistent with chemical exchange arising from the conformational dynamics of the αC-helix.
source: The short relaxation time of the αC-inbroad resonance (<5 ms) is consistent with chemical exchange arising from the conformational dynamics of the αC-helix.
evidence: This is inferred from T2 relaxation measurements shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The αC-in^broad resonance was not observed in BRAF samples with dimer-disrupting interface mutations.
source: (3) the αC-inbroad resonance was not observed in BRAF samples with dimer-disrupting interface mutations (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c)
evidence: This is a direct observation from 19F NMR experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c.

claim: D2O exchange experiments revealed large and nearly identical isotope shifts for the αC-in^narrow and αC-in^broad resonances (0.047 vs 0.050 ppm).
source: (4) D2O exchange experiments revealed large and nearly identical isotope shifts for the αC-innarrow and αC-inbroad resonances (0.047 vs 0.050 ppm), indicating a similar degree of solvent exposure of the probe, compared to a relatively small shift for the αC-out monomer peak (0.019 ppm) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: This is measured from D2O exchange experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1f.

claim: As the experimental temperature was raised from 2°C to 34°C, the αC-in^broad peak width decreased.
source: Furthermore, as the experimental temperature was raised from 2°C to 34°C, the αC-inbroad peak width decreased, consistent with faster exchange kinetics arising from increased conformational dynamics (Figure 4c and d).
evidence: This is a direct observation from variable-temperature 19F NMR experiments shown in Figure 4c,d.

claim: As temperature increased, the αC-in^broad peak area decreased and the αC-in^narrow peak area increased in a reciprocal manner.
source: At the same time, the αC-inbroad peak area decreased and the αC-innarrow peak area increased in a reciprocal manner, indicating a shifting equilibrium between the two dimeric states (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is a direct observation from variable-temperature 19F NMR experiments shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The individual subunits of the BRAF dimer transition between two states with strikingly different dynamics.
source: The individual subunits of the BRAF dimer transition between two states with strikingly different dynamics. In one state, the subunit is locked in the αC-in conformation, with the αC-helix relatively static (αC-innarrow). In the other, more dynamic state, the αC-helix undergoes transitions between conformational substates (αC-inbroad).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on 19F NMR data shown in Figure 4.

claim: BRAF dimers are not constrained in a symmetrical αC-in/αC-in configuration.
source: This indicates that BRAF dimers are not constrained in a symmetrical αC-in/αC-in configuration, as structural models suggest (Park et al., 2019; Liau et al., 2020), but rather that one subunit is free to explore other conformations.
evidence: This is inferred from 19F NMR data showing the presence of the dynamic αC-in^broad state.

claim: The binding of a single type II inhibitor molecule can dramatically increase BRAF dimerization because the BRAF dimer only requires one subunit to adopt the locked αC-in conformation.
source: This explains how the binding of a single type II inhibitor molecule, which pays the energetic penalty for locking one BRAF subunit in the αC-in state, can dramatically increase BRAF dimerization, since the BRAF dimer only requires one and not both subunits to adopt the locked αC-in conformation.
evidence: This is an interpretation that connects the NMR findings with the allosteric coupling results.

claim: The dynamic heterogeneity of the BRAF dimer revealed by NMR may form the foundation for the asymmetric allosteric coupling that gives rise to paradoxical activation of BRAF by type II inhibitors.
source: Thus, the dynamic heterogeneity of the BRAF dimer revealed by NMR may form the foundation for the asymmetric allosteric coupling that gives rise to paradoxical activation of BRAF by type II inhibitors.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanistic interpretation connecting NMR data with allosteric coupling and paradoxical activation.

claim: Both FDA-approved αC-out RAF inhibitors and newer αC-in RAF inhibitors trigger paradoxical activation of BRAF.
source: The FDA-approved αC-out RAF inhibitors and the newer αC-in RAF inhibitors currently under development represent fundamentally different classes of drug that have opposite effects on RAF conformation and dimerization. Nonetheless, both drug classes trigger paradoxical activation of BRAF.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of known phenomena.

claim: Activation by αC-out inhibitors is attributed in part to negative allostery.
source: Activation by the αC-out inhibitors is attributed in part to negative allostery, where dimer-disrupting allosteric effects prevent full occupancy of intact dimers (Karoulia et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: The model of negative allostery does not provide an adequate explanation for paradoxical activation by αC-in inhibitors.
source: This model of negative allostery does not provide an adequate explanation for paradoxical activation by αC-in inhibitors, which are positively coupled to dimerization and have been thought to bind both subunits of the dimer with equal potency (Cotto-Rios et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as motivation for the study.

claim: For type II inhibitors, favorable allostery occurs through an asymmetric coupling mechanism in which the binding of the first inhibitor molecule promotes dimerization much more strongly than binding of the second inhibitor molecule.
source: Remarkably, for type II inhibitors this favorable allostery is not evenly distributed between both binding sites of the dimer, as previously proposed (Cotto-Rios et al., 2020), and instead occurs through an asymmetric coupling mechanism in which the binding of the first inhibitor molecule promotes dimerization much more strongly than binding of the second inhibitor molecule.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding stated in the Discussion.

claim: Allosteric asymmetry triggers selective induction of BRAF dimers with only one subunit bound to inhibitor.
source: We demonstrate that this allosteric asymmetry triggers selective induction of BRAF dimers with only one subunit bound to inhibitor, with larger degrees of asymmetry leading to greater induction of these partially occupied dimers.
evidence: This is a summary of findings stated in the Discussion.

claim: The degree of induction of partially occupied dimers fully accounts for both the concentration dependence and amplitude of BRAF activation measured in vitro for 11 different αC-in inhibitors.
source: Indeed, the degree of induction of partially occupied dimers fully accounts for both the concentration dependence and amplitude of BRAF activation measured in vitro for 11 different αC-in inhibitors.
evidence: This is a summary of findings stated in the Discussion, supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Type I inhibitors lack sufficient allosteric coupling asymmetry to induce paradoxical activation through BRAF homodimers.
source: While type II inhibitors are asymmetrically coupled and strongly activate BRAF homodimers, type I inhibitors lack sufficient allosteric coupling asymmetry to induce paradoxical activation through this mechanism.
evidence: This is a summary of findings stated in the Discussion.

claim: Type I inhibitors induce paradoxical activation through BRAF:CRAF heterodimers.
source: We demonstrate, however, that type I inhibitors induce MAPK pathway activation in melanoma cells, consistent with previous reports (Poulikakos et al., 2010; Hatzivassiliou et al., 2010; Heidorn et al., 2010). These observations point to type I inhibitors inducing paradoxical activation through BRAF:CRAF heterodimers, rather than BRAF homodimers, a hypothesis that is consistent with a large body of published work (Hatzivassiliou et al., 2010; Karoulia et al., 2016; Jin et al., 2017; Heidorn et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Type I inhibitors bind less tightly to CRAF than BRAF.
source: Because type I inhibitors bind less tightly to CRAF than BRAF, the subunits of a heterodimer will have inherently different drug affinities, providing a window for paradoxical activation in the absence of allosteric asymmetry.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an explanation for type I inhibitor activation.

claim: The emergence of clinical resistance to belvarafenib and naporafenib can be mediated by induction of ARAF.
source: In particular, the emergence of clinical resistance to belvarafenib and another type II inhibitor, naporafenib, can be mediated by induction of ARAF (Yen et al., 2021; Tkacik et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Both belvarafenib and naporafenib bind ARAF less potently than BRAF.
source: Since both belvarafenib and naporafenib bind ARAF less potently than BRAF, the disparity in drug affinities for the first and second subunits of ARAF/BRAF heterodimers is likely further boosted over that arising from asymmetric allosteric coupling alone, sustaining activation at higher drug concentrations and conferring resistance.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of resistance mechanisms.

claim: Type I and type II inhibitors stabilize distinct αC-helix conformations in solution.
source: We show that type I and type II inhibitors stabilize distinct αC-helix conformations in solution.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a summary of DEER results.

claim: Type II inhibitors trigger a structural change of the catalytic DFG-motif and activation loop of BRAF that is not accomplished by type I inhibitors.
source: In addition, type II inhibitors trigger a structural change of the catalytic DFG-motif and activation loop of BRAF that is not accomplished by type I inhibitors.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as known structural information.

claim: The recent cryo-EM structure of dimeric BRAF in complex with 14-3-3 shows an asymmetric arrangement of the BRAF dimer with respect to 14-3-3.
source: The recent cryo-EM structure of dimeric BRAF in complex with the scaffolding protein 14-3-3, determined in the absence of inhibitors, shows an asymmetric arrangement of the BRAF dimer with respect to 14-3-3 (Kondo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: In the cryo-EM structure, the C-terminal tail of one BRAF subunit binds to and blocks the active site of the opposite subunit, while the reciprocal interaction is prevented.
source: This arrangement permits the C-terminal tail of one subunit to bind to and block the active site of the opposite subunit, while the reciprocal interaction is prevented.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion describing the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Several type II inhibitors including belvarafenib and LY3009120 have entered clinical trials.
source: Several type II inhibitors studied here including belvarafenib (NCT04835805) and LY3009120 (NCT02014116) have entered clinical trials or could be repurposed like the FDA-approved chronic myeloid leukemia drug ponatinib.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as clinical context.

claim: Paradoxical activation by type II inhibitors has been observed in cell lines both with and without elevated RAS activity.
source: However, paradoxical activation by these type II inhibitors has been observed in cell lines both with and without elevated RAS activity (Poulikakos et al., 2010; Karoulia et al., 2016; Yen et al., 2021; Cotto-Rios et al., 2020; Lai et al., 2022; Lavoie et al., 2013), and demonstrated to trigger expression of ERK target genes and increased cell proliferation (Lai et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Ponatinib can activate ERK in RAS-mutant cells at concentrations as low as 1 nM.
source: We along with others show that ponatinib can activate ERK in RAS-mutant cells at concentrations as low as 1 nM, and that this activation is only suppressed at concentrations above 1 μM (Cotto-Rios et al., 2020), higher than the plasma level achievable in patients (Ye et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Belvarafenib increases MAPK signaling over a concentration range similar to other type II inhibitors like LY3009120.
source: Similarly, while belvarafenib has shown promising activity in preclinical and clinical studies (Yen et al., 2021), it increases MAPK signaling over a concentration range similar to other type II inhibitors like LY3009120, which has shown an unexpected lack of clinical efficacy (Sullivan et al., 2020) despite favorable preclinical results (Peng et al., 2015; Yen et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.
